more.title: More of the French Sentence
more.desc: One word is missing from a French sentence: a verb in another person, an object or stressed pronoun, à with the person who receives, de with the possessor, a word joined by et, or a word of place. The word is chosen from tiles at the first levels and written at the higher ones.

intro.h: Persons. French writes the subject pronoun, because many endings sound alike, and the verb agrees with its subject.
eg: nous portons le livre; tu parles au roi

intro.h: The pronoun. An object pronoun stands before the verb, and after a preposition French uses the stressed form: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles.
eg: le roi me voit; le livre est pour moi

intro.h: À and de. French has no dative or genitive case on the noun. The person who receives is introduced by à, and the possessor by de, and both contract with le and les: au, aux, du, des.
eg: le roi donne le livre au juge; le livre du roi est bon

intro.h: Et. Two subjects joined by et take a plural verb, and an adjective that describes a masculine and a feminine noun together is masculine plural.
eg: le roi et la reine sont contents

intro.h: Place. À stands before a city, en before a feminine country, au before a masculine one, and aux before a plural one; de shows motion from.
eg: à Paris, en France, au Canada, aux États-Unis; il vient de Paris

items.en: We carry the book.
items.why: The subject is nous, the first person plural, and the ending -ons marks that person. Porte is singular, portez is the second person plural, and portent is the third person plural.

items.en: You (one friend) speak to the king.
items.why: Tu is the second person singular, and a verb in -er ends in -es in that person. Parle is the first or third person singular, and parlez and parlons are plural.

items.en: They finish the letter.
items.why: Ils is the third person plural, and finir, a verb of the second group, adds -iss- in the plural: finissent. Finit and finis are singular, and finissons is the first person plural.

items.en: I sell the horse.
items.why: Je is the first person singular, and vendre ends in -s in that person. Vend is the third person singular, and vendons and vendez are plural.

items.en: You (more than one) are in the garden.
items.why: Vous is the second person plural, and the form of être for that person is êtes. Sommes is the first person plural, sont the third person plural, and est the third person singular.

items.en: The queen has a garden.
items.why: La reine is a third person singular subject, and the form of avoir for that person is a. As and ai are the second and first person singular, and ont is plural.

items.en: We go to the city.
items.why: Nous is the first person plural, and the form of aller for that person is allons. Allez is the second person plural, vont the third person plural, and va the third person singular.

items.en: The friends come from the city.
items.why: Les amis is a third person plural subject, and the form of venir for that person is viennent. Vient is singular, and venons and venez are the first and second persons plural.

items.en: The king sees me.
items.why: Me is the object pronoun of the first person, and it stands before the verb. Moi is the stressed form, used after a preposition or alone, je is the subject, and mon is the possessive.

items.en: The king sees her.
items.why: The direct object pronoun for a feminine singular person or thing is la, and it stands before the verb. Le would mean him, elle is the subject or stressed form, and lui is the indirect object.

items.en: The queen gives him the book.
items.why: The king receives the book, so he is the indirect object, and the indirect object pronoun of the third person singular is lui. Le is the direct object, il the subject, and leur is plural.

items.en: The queen gives them the book.
items.why: The indirect object pronoun of the third person plural is leur, and it never takes an s. Lui is singular, les is the direct object, and leurs is the possessive adjective before a plural noun.

items.en: The book is for me.
items.why: After a preposition French uses the stressed pronoun, so pour moi. Me is the object pronoun, which stands before a verb, and je is the subject.

items.en: I see them (the horses).
items.why: The horses are the direct object, and the direct object pronoun of the third person plural is les. Leur is the indirect object, eux is the stressed form, and lui is singular.

items.en: The man sees us.
items.why: The object pronoun of the first person plural is nous, the same form as the subject, and it stands before the verb. Notre and nos are possessives, and on is a subject pronoun.

items.en: He speaks with them (the men).
items.why: After a preposition French uses the stressed pronoun, and the stressed form of the third person plural masculine is eux. Leur and les are object pronouns, and ils is the subject.

items.en: The king gives the book to the friend.
items.fr: Le roi donne le livre ______ ami.
items.why: Ami begins with a vowel, so the article is l’, and à l’ does not contract. Au is à and le, which is used before a consonant, and aux is plural.

items.en: The king gives the book to the queen.
items.fr: Le roi donne le livre ______ reine.
items.why: The person who receives is introduced by à, and reine is feminine, so the form is à la, which does not contract. Au is masculine, and aux is plural.

items.en: The king gives the book to the friends.
items.fr: Le roi donne le livre ______ amis.
items.why: À and les contract to aux before a plural noun. Au is singular, à les is never written, and des is de and les.

items.en: The woman sends a letter to the king.
items.fr: La femme envoie une lettre ______ roi.
items.why: The king receives the letter, so he is introduced by à, and à and le contract to au. Du is de and le, and à le is never written.

items.en: The king speaks to the women.
items.why: Parler takes à before the person spoken to, and à and les contract to aux. Des is de and les, and au is singular.

items.en: We give a gift to the man.
items.why: Homme begins with a mute h, so the article is l’, and à l’ does not contract. Au is used before a consonant, and de l’ would mean of the man.

items.en: He sends gifts to the kings.
items.why: À and les contract to aux. Au is singular, and des is de and les.

items.en: The queen gives the horse to the woman.
items.fr: La reine donne le cheval ______ femme.
items.why: Femme is feminine, so the person who receives is introduced by à la, which does not contract. De la would mean of the woman.

items.en: The king’s book is good.
items.why: French shows the possessor with de, and de and le contract to du. Des is plural, and au is à and le.

items.en: The queen’s house is large.
items.why: The possessor is introduced by de, and reine is feminine, so the form is de la, which does not contract. Du is masculine, and à la would mean to the queen.

items.en: The friends’ garden is small.
items.why: De and les contract to des before a plural noun. Du is singular, de les is never written, and aux is à and les.

items.en: The man’s horse is old.
items.why: Homme begins with a mute h, so the article is l’, and de l’ does not contract. Du is used before a consonant, and à l’ would mean to the man.

items.en: The women’s letters are long.
items.why: De and les contract to des. De les is never written, du is singular, and aux is à and les.

items.en: The king’s gifts are beautiful.
items.why: There is one king, so the form is du, de and le contracted. Des would mean of the kings, and au is à and le.

items.en: The city’s gardens are large.
items.why: Ville is feminine and singular, so the possessor is introduced by de la. Du is masculine, des is plural, and à la would mean to the city.

items.en: The friend’s table is small.
items.why: Ami begins with a vowel, so the article is l’, and de l’ does not contract. Du is used before a consonant.

items.en: The king and the queen carry the gift.
items.fr: Le roi et la reine ______ le cadeau.
items.why: Two subjects joined by et make a plural subject of the third person, so the verb is portent. Porte is singular, and portons and portez are the first and second persons.

items.en: The king and the queen are content.
items.fr: Le roi et la reine sont ______.
items.why: An adjective that describes a masculine noun and a feminine noun together is masculine plural: contents. Contentes would describe only feminine nouns.

items.en: The woman and the girl are small.
items.fr: La femme et la fille sont ______.
items.why: Both nouns are feminine, so the adjective is feminine plural: petites. Petits is masculine plural, and petite is singular.

items.en: You and I speak to the king.
items.fr: Toi et moi, nous ______ au roi.
items.why: A subject that includes the speaker is of the first person, and toi et moi is plural, so the verb is parlons. Parlez is the second person plural, and parlent the third.

items.en: My friend and I go to the city.
items.fr: Mon ami et moi ______ à la ville.
items.why: Mon ami et moi includes the speaker, so the verb is in the first person plural: allons. Vont is the third person plural, and allez the second.

items.en: The man and the horse are old.
items.why: Both nouns are masculine, and vieux is both the masculine singular and the masculine plural. Vieille and vieilles are feminine, and vieil stands only before a singular noun that begins with a vowel.

items.en: The king sends the book and the letter.
items.fr: Le roi envoie le livre et ______ lettre.
items.why: In French each noun keeps its own article, and lettre is feminine and singular, so la. Le is masculine, and les is plural.

items.en: Peter and Mary sell the house.
items.why: Two subjects joined by et make a plural subject of the third person, so vendent. Vend and vends are singular, and vendons is the first person plural.

items.en: The king lives in Paris.
items.why: Before the name of a city French uses à for place where and for place to which. En is used before a feminine country, and au before a masculine country.

items.en: The queen goes to France.
items.why: Before a feminine country French uses en, without the article. À is used before a city, au before a masculine country, and aux before a plural one.

items.en: The friend lives in Canada.
items.why: Canada is a masculine country that begins with a consonant, so French uses au, à and le contracted. En is used before a feminine country.

items.en: The king goes to the United States.
items.why: États-Unis is plural, so French uses aux, à and les contracted. Au is singular, and à les is never written.

items.en: The letter is in the book.
items.why: Dans with the article means inside something: dans le livre. En is used without an article, as in en France, and au livre would mean to the book.

items.en: The man comes from Paris.
items.why: Motion from a city is shown by de: il vient de Paris. À would mean to Paris, and du is de and le, which a city name does not take.

items.en: The woman comes from France.
items.why: Motion from a feminine country is shown by de without the article: elle vient de France. Du is used before a masculine country, and en would mean in France.

items.en: The friend comes from Canada.
items.why: Motion from a masculine country is shown by de with the article, and de and le contract to du. Au would mean to Canada, and des is plural.

voice.title: The Passive, the Infinitive, and the Participle in French
voice.desc: One word is missing from a French sentence: a passive participle, the doer, on or a pronominal verb, an infinitive with its preposition, or a participle that agrees.

intro.h: The passive. The passive is être with the past participle, which agrees with the subject, and the doer is introduced by par. French also uses on, or a pronominal verb, where English uses a passive.
eg: la lettre est écrite par le roi; on parle français; ce livre se vend bien

intro.h: The infinitive. Some verbs take the infinitive directly, such as vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, and aller; others take à or de before it.
eg: je veux lire; il commence à écrire; elle essaie de comprendre

intro.h: The participle. With être the past participle agrees with the subject; with avoir it agrees only with a direct object that stands before it. En with the present participle says that two actions go on together.
eg: la reine est venue; la lettre que j’ai écrite; en lisant

items.en: The letter is written by the king.
items.fr: La lettre est ______ par le roi.
items.why: In the passive the past participle agrees with the subject, and lettre is feminine and singular, so écrite. Écrit is masculine, and écrits and écrites are plural.

items.en: The books are sold by the friend.
items.why: The passive is être with the past participle, and the participle agrees with the subject, here masculine plural: vendus.

items.en: The house is sold by the woman.
items.fr: La maison est ______ par la femme.
items.why: Maison is feminine and singular, so the participle of the passive is vendue.

items.en: The horse is seen by the queen.
items.fr: Le cheval est vu ______ la reine.
items.why: The doer in a French passive is usually introduced by par. Pour means for, and à means to.

items.en: The queens are loved by the king.
items.fr: Les reines sont ______ par le roi.
items.why: The participle agrees with the subject, reines, which is feminine plural: aimées.

items.en: French is spoken here.
items.why: French often uses on with an active verb where English uses a passive, and on takes the third person singular: on parle. Parlé is the participle.

items.en: This book sells well.
items.why: A pronominal verb can have a sense close to the passive, as in se vendre, to be sold. Se is not elided here, because vend begins with a consonant.

items.en: The queen washes herself.
items.why: A pronominal verb takes a reflexive pronoun of the same person as the subject, and for the third person that pronoun is se. La would mean that she washes someone else.

items.en: I want to read the book.
items.why: Vouloir is followed directly by the infinitive: je veux lire. Lis is the present, lu the past participle, and lisant the present participle.

items.en: He can finish the letter.
items.why: Pouvoir is followed directly by the infinitive: il peut finir. Finit is the present, and fini the past participle.

items.en: We are going to sell the house.
items.why: Aller with an infinitive makes the near future: nous allons vendre. The infinitive does not change for person.

items.en: He begins to write.
items.why: Commencer takes à before an infinitive: il commence à écrire. Each verb has its own preposition before the infinitive, and the dictionary gives it.

items.en: She tries to understand.
items.why: Essayer takes de before an infinitive: elle essaie de comprendre.

items.en: The king must leave.
items.why: Devoir is followed directly by the infinitive: il doit partir. Part is the present, and parti the past participle.

items.en: He works in order to buy a house.
items.why: Pour with the infinitive gives the purpose of the action, when the subject of the two verbs is the same: pour acheter.

items.en: She forgets to close the door.
items.why: Oublier takes de before an infinitive: elle oublie de fermer la porte.

items.en: The queen has come.
items.why: Venir forms the passé composé with être, and then the participle agrees with the subject, here feminine singular: venue.

items.en: The friends (men) have arrived.
items.why: Arriver takes être, and the participle agrees with the subject, here masculine plural: arrivés.

items.en: The women went to the city.
items.fr: Les femmes sont ______ à la ville.
items.why: Aller takes être, so the participle agrees with les femmes, feminine plural: allées.

items.en: The queen has spoken.
items.why: Parler forms the passé composé with avoir, and then the participle does not agree with the subject: elle a parlé.

items.en: The letter that I wrote is long.
items.fr: La lettre que j’ai ______ est longue.
items.why: With avoir the participle agrees with a direct object that stands before it. Here que stands for la lettre, which is feminine, so écrite.

items.en: While reading the book, he learns.
items.why: En with the present participle, the gérondif, says that two actions go on at the same time: en lisant.

items.en: a letter written by the king
items.why: A past participle used as an adjective agrees with its noun, and lettre is feminine: une lettre écrite.

items.en: The queen washed herself.
items.why: A pronominal verb takes être, and here the participle agrees with the reflexive pronoun, which stands for the queen: lavée.

clause.title: Clauses and the Participle in French
clause.desc: One word is missing from a French sentence: a relative pronoun, a word in a clause of cause, a word in a condition with si, a word in a reported statement or question, or a participle.

intro.h: The relative. Qui is the subject of its clause, que the object, dont replaces de with a noun, and où stands for a place or a time.
eg: l’homme qui parle; le livre que je lis; le livre dont je parle; la ville où j’habite

intro.h: Cause. Parce que and comme give a reason as a fact, and their verb is in the indicative.
eg: il reste parce qu’il est malade

intro.h: Condition. A real condition takes si with the present and a future in the result; a condition that is not real takes si with the imparfait and a conditional in the result. After si meaning if, French uses neither the future nor the conditional.
eg: si tu viens, je serai content; si j’avais le livre, je le lirais

intro.h: Reported speech. A reported statement begins with que, a reported yes-or-no question with si, and a reported question about a thing with ce que or ce qui.
eg: il dit que le roi est malade; je ne sais pas s’il vient; il demande ce que tu veux

intro.h: The participle. En with the present participle gives the time, the manner, or the means of the main action.
eg: en lisant, il apprend; il est entré en chantant

items.en: The man who speaks is my friend.
items.why: The relative is the subject of parle, and the subject relative is qui. Que is the object, dont replaces de with a noun, and où is a place or a time.

items.en: The book that I read is long.
items.fr: Le livre ______ je lis est long.
items.why: The relative is the object of lis, and the object relative is que. Qui would be the subject.

items.en: The city where I live is large.
items.why: The relative stands for a place, so où.

items.en: The book I am speaking about is old.
items.fr: Le livre ______ je parle est vieux.
items.why: Parler takes de before the thing spoken of, and the relative that replaces de with its noun is dont.

items.en: The woman whom the king sees is the queen.
items.fr: La femme ______ le roi voit est la reine.
items.why: Le roi is the subject of voit, and the relative is its object, so que.

items.en: The horses that run are beautiful.
items.why: The relative is the subject of courent, so qui. The verb then agrees with the antecedent, les chevaux.

items.en: The day when he came was long.
items.fr: Le jour ______ il est venu était long.
items.why: After a noun of time French uses où as the relative: le jour où il est venu.

items.en: The friend whose house is large lives here.
items.fr: L’ami ______ la maison est grande habite ici.
items.why: The house belongs to the friend, so the relative replaces de with a noun: la maison de l’ami becomes dont la maison.

items.en: He stays because he is ill.
items.why: Parce que gives a fact as the reason, and its verb is in the indicative: il est. Soit is the subjunctive.

items.en: She reads because she has the time.
items.fr: Elle lit parce qu’elle ______ le temps.
items.why: After parce que the verb is in the indicative, so elle a. Ait is the subjunctive.

items.en: We stay because it is raining.
items.why: The reason is stated as a fact, so the indicative: il pleut. Pleuve is the subjunctive.

items.en: They leave because the king is coming.
items.fr: Ils partent parce que le roi ______.
items.why: After parce que the verb is in the indicative: le roi vient. Vienne is the subjunctive.

items.en: He stays because he is tired.
items.why: The clause gives the reason, so parce que. Pour que and afin que give a purpose, and bien que a concession, and all three take the subjunctive.

items.en: Since the king is ill, the queen speaks.
items.fr: ______ le roi est malade, la reine parle.
items.why: Comme at the head of the sentence gives the cause, and its verb is in the indicative. Pour que and afin que give a purpose, and bien que a concession.

items.en: She is happy because she has won.
items.fr: Elle est heureuse parce qu’elle ______ gagné.
items.why: After parce que the verb is in the indicative, and the passé composé of gagner is made with avoir: elle a gagné.

items.en: If I had the book, I would read it.
items.fr: Si j’______ le livre, je le lirais.
items.why: A condition that is not real is given by si with the imparfait, and the result is in the conditional. After si meaning if, French does not use the conditional.

items.en: If I had the book, I would read it.
items.fr: Si j’avais le livre, je le ______.
items.why: After si with the imparfait, the result is in the conditional: je lirais. Lirai is the future.

items.en: If he were king, he would be happy.
items.why: The condition is not real, so si takes the imparfait: s’il était roi. Serait is the conditional, which stands in the result.

items.en: If you come, I will be content.
items.why: A real condition about the future takes si with the present, and the result is in the future. After si meaning if, French uses neither the future nor the conditional.

items.en: If you come, I will be content.
items.why: After si with the present, the result about the future is in the future: je serai. Serais is the conditional, which follows si with the imparfait.

items.en: If the queen spoke, the king would listen.
items.fr: Si la reine parlait, le roi ______.
items.why: After si with the imparfait, the result is in the conditional: le roi écouterait.

items.en: If we had the time, we would go to Paris.
items.fr: Si nous ______ le temps, nous irions à Paris.
items.why: The condition is not real, so si takes the imparfait: nous avions. Aurions is the conditional.

items.en: He says that the king is ill.
items.fr: Il dit ______ le roi est malade.
items.why: A reported statement after dire is introduced by que, and French never leaves que out.

items.en: I do not know whether he is coming.
items.why: A reported yes-or-no question is introduced by si, and si is elided before il: s’il. Si il is never written.

items.en: He asks what you want.
items.why: A reported question about the object of the verb is introduced by ce que. Ce qui is used when the word asked about is the subject.

items.en: He asks what is happening.
items.why: The word asked about is the subject of se passe, so the reported question is introduced by ce qui.

items.en: I ask where the king is.
items.why: A reported question keeps its question word: où est le roi becomes je demande où est le roi.

items.en: She knows that the queen has come.
items.fr: Elle sait que la reine ______ venue.
items.why: After savoir que the verb is in the indicative, and venir forms the passé composé with être: la reine est venue.

items.en: I think that he is right.
items.why: After an affirmative verb of thinking, such as penser, the reported statement is in the indicative: il a raison.

items.en: I do not think that he is right.
items.fr: Je ne pense pas qu’il ______ raison.
items.why: After a verb of thinking in the negative, written French usually puts the reported statement in the subjunctive: qu’il ait raison.

items.en: While reading, he learns.
items.why: The gérondif is en with the present participle, and it says that two actions go on together: en lisant.

items.en: He came in singing.
items.why: En with the present participle gives the manner of the action: il est entré en chantant.

items.en: Having finished the letter, the king left.
items.fr: Ayant ______ la lettre, le roi est parti.
items.why: Ayant with the past participle presents one action as complete before the next: ayant fini.

items.en: It is by working that one succeeds.
items.why: The gérondif, en with the present participle, gives the means: en travaillant.

items.en: Once the letter was written, the king sent it.
items.fr: Une fois la lettre ______, le roi l’a envoyée.
items.why: The participle in this phrase agrees with its noun, lettre, which is feminine: une fois la lettre écrite.

items.en: Seeing the king, the woman stopped.
items.fr: ______ le roi, la femme s’est arrêtée.
items.why: The present participle, without en, can open a sentence and give the circumstance of the main action: voyant le roi.

mood.title: The Subjunctive, the Conditional, and the Imperative
mood.desc: One word is missing from a French sentence, or one form of a verb is asked for: the present subjunctive, the subjunctive after il faut que, pour que, or bien que, the conditional, or the imperative.

intro.h: The subjunctive. The present subjunctive takes its stem from the third person plural of the present and adds -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent. Être, avoir, aller, faire, and pouvoir are irregular.
eg: que je finisse, que je sois, qu’il ait, que j’aille

intro.h: Its uses. The subjunctive follows a verb of wanting or of feeling with que, il faut que, pour que, bien que, and avant que. An affirmative verb of thinking takes the indicative.
eg: il faut que tu viennes; bien qu’il soit malade; je pense qu’il vient

intro.h: The conditional. The conditional is made from the stem of the future and the endings of the imparfait. It gives the result of a condition that is not real, and it softens a request.
eg: je parlerais; si j’étais riche, j’achèterais une maison; je voudrais un livre

intro.h: The imperative. The imperative has three forms and no subject pronoun. A verb in -er has no s in the second person singular, and in the affirmative an object pronoun follows the verb.
eg: lis, lisons, lisez; parle au roi; donne-moi le livre

items.en: Present subjunctive, first person singular, of “finir.”
items.why: The present subjunctive takes its stem from the third person plural of the present, finissent, and adds -e: que je finisse.

items.en: Present subjunctive, first person singular, of “être.”
items.why: Être has an irregular subjunctive: que je sois. Suis is the present indicative, and serai the future.

items.en: Present subjunctive, third person singular, of “avoir.”
items.why: Avoir has an irregular subjunctive: qu’il ait. A is the present indicative, and aura the future.

items.en: Present subjunctive, first person singular, of “aller.”
items.why: Aller has the subjunctive que j’aille. Vais is the present indicative, and irai the future.

items.en: Present subjunctive, third person plural, of “faire.”
items.why: Faire has the subjunctive stem fass-: qu’ils fassent. Font is the present indicative.

items.en: Present subjunctive, first person plural, of “venir.”
items.why: In the first and second persons plural the subjunctive of venir takes the stem ven- and the endings -ions and -iez: que nous venions.

items.en: Present subjunctive, third person singular, of “pouvoir.”
items.why: Pouvoir has the subjunctive stem puiss-: qu’il puisse. Peut is the present indicative.

items.en: Present subjunctive, second person plural, of “être.”
items.why: The subjunctive of être in the second person plural is que vous soyez. Êtes is the present indicative.

items.en: It is necessary that you come.
items.why: Il faut que requires the subjunctive: que tu viennes. Viens is the indicative.

items.en: I want you to be happy.
items.why: After a verb of wanting with que and a different subject, French uses the subjunctive: que tu sois.

items.en: He speaks slowly so that the queen may understand.
items.fr: Il parle lentement pour que la reine ______.
items.why: Pour que gives a purpose and requires the subjunctive: qu’elle comprenne.

items.en: Although he is ill, he works.
items.why: Bien que gives a concession and requires the subjunctive: bien qu’il soit.

items.en: Leave before the king comes!
items.why: Avant que requires the subjunctive: avant que le roi vienne.

items.en: I am glad that you are here.
items.fr: Je suis content que vous ______ là.
items.why: After an expression of feeling with que, French uses the subjunctive: que vous soyez là.

items.en: I think that he is coming.
items.why: An affirmative verb of thinking states what the speaker holds to be so, and it takes the indicative: il vient.

items.en: It is necessary that we finish the letter.
items.fr: Il faut que nous ______ la lettre.
items.why: Il faut que requires the subjunctive, and the first person plural of the subjunctive ends in -ions: que nous finissions.

items.en: I would like a book, please.
items.fr: Je ______ un livre, s’il vous plaît.
items.why: The conditional softens a request: je voudrais. Voudrai is the future, and voudrait the third person.

items.en: Conditional, first person singular, of “avoir.”
items.why: The conditional takes the stem of the future, aur-, and the endings of the imparfait: j’aurais. Aurai is the future.

items.en: Conditional, third person singular, of “être.”
items.why: The conditional of être is made on the future stem ser- with the ending -ait: il serait.

items.en: Conditional, first person plural, of “faire.”
items.why: The future stem of faire is fer-, and the conditional adds -ions: nous ferions. Ferons is the future, faisions the imparfait, and fassions the subjunctive.

items.en: Conditional, second person singular, of “pouvoir.”
items.why: The future stem of pouvoir is pourr-, and the conditional adds -ais: tu pourrais.

items.en: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
items.fr: Si j’étais riche, j’______ une maison.
items.why: After si with the imparfait, the result is in the conditional: j’achèterais. Achèterai is the future.

items.en: Could you help me?
items.why: The conditional makes a polite request: pourriez-vous m’aider ? Pourrez is the future.

items.en: Conditional, third person plural, of “parler.”
items.why: The conditional of a verb in -er is the infinitive with the endings of the imparfait: ils parleraient.

items.en: (To one friend) Read the book!
items.why: The imperative has no subject pronoun, and the form for one person addressed as tu is lis. Lisons means let us read.

items.en: (To several people) Finish the work!
items.why: The imperative addressed to several people is the vous form without the pronoun: finissez.

items.en: Let us go to the city!
items.why: The imperative of the first person plural includes the speaker: allons, let us go.

items.en: (To one friend) Speak to the king!
items.why: A verb in -er has no s in the imperative of the second person singular: parle.

items.en: (To one friend) Give me the book!
items.why: In the affirmative imperative the object pronoun follows the verb, and me becomes moi: donne-moi.

items.en: (To one child) Be good!
items.why: Être has an irregular imperative, taken from the subjunctive: sois, soyons, soyez.

items.en: (To several people) Do not speak!
items.why: A negative imperative puts ne before the verb and pas after it: ne parlez pas.

items.en: (To one friend) Come here!
items.why: The imperative of the second person singular of venir is viens, the same as the present without tu.
